title: Messages API basics
summary: Every Messages API call passes a list of `user`/`assistant` turns and an output cap, `max_tokens`, and can include a top-level `system` prompt. Each response tells you why Claude stopped through `stop_reason`, and your code has to branch on it.
keyPoints: Put instructions and roles in the top-level **`system`** parameter; a `system` message can't open `messages`.
`max_tokens` is an absolute ceiling on **output** tokens; the model may stop before it.
`stop_reason: "max_tokens"` means the reply was truncated: raise `max_tokens` or continue the response.
`stop_reason: "tool_use"` means Claude wants **you** to run a tool and send back a `tool_result`.
`end_turn` is the normal finish: use the response.

sections.heading: The shape of a request
sections.body:
A request names a model, sets `max_tokens`, and passes `messages`: alternating `user` and `assistant` turns. Consecutive turns with the same role are combined into one turn.

Context and standing instructions, such as a goal or a role, go in the top-level `system` parameter. Even a single sentence of role in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone.

sections.heading: Reading stop_reason
sections.body:
Every response carries a `stop_reason`:

- `end_turn`: Claude finished naturally. Use the response.
- `max_tokens`: the response reached your limit. Raise `max_tokens` or continue the response.
- `stop_sequence`: Claude emitted one of your `stop_sequences`.
- `tool_use`: Claude is calling a tool. Run the tool and return the result.
- `refusal`: Claude declined to respond. Read `stop_details`.

sections.heading: The tool-use loop
sections.body:
For tools your app defines, the model never executes anything itself. When the response stops with `tool_use`, your code runs each tool and sends a new request whose last message is a `user` turn of `tool_result` blocks.

Repeat while `stop_reason` is `tool_use`. Any other stop reason exits the loop.

title: Understanding requirements
summary: Turning a business need into an LLM solution means checking that Claude fits the task, setting success criteria you can measure, and choosing a starting model by your constraints. The rule to remember: define specific, measurable criteria and a way to test them before you prompt.
keyPoints: Good success criteria are **specific, measurable, achievable and relevant**; even hazy goals like safety can be quantified.
Most use cases need **multidimensional** criteria, such as accuracy plus toxicity plus response time.
Claude suits classification when labeled data is **scarce** (a few dozen examples), categories change, or rules are semantic.
Tight latency, cost-sensitive, high-volume work: start **efficiency-first** with Claude Haiku 5.5 and upgrade only if needed.
Not every failing criterion is a prompt problem: latency and cost can sometimes improve more easily by **selecting a different model**.

sections.heading: Write measurable success criteria
sections.body:
Building a successful LLM application starts with clearly defining your success criteria, then designing evaluations to measure performance against them. Good criteria are:

- Specific: "accurate sentiment classification", not "good performance"
- Measurable: quantitative metrics or well-defined qualitative scales
- Achievable: based on benchmarks, prior experiments, AI research or expert knowledge
- Relevant: aligned with the app's purpose and user needs

Even hazy topics can be quantified: instead of "safe outputs", aim for less than 0.1% of outputs out of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity by the content filter.

Most use cases need several criteria at once. The guide's good example, on a held-out test set of 10,000 diverse posts: an F1 score of at least 0.85, 99.5% of outputs non-toxic, and 95% response time < 200ms.

sections.heading: Decide whether Claude fits
sections.body:
Anthropic's ticket-routing guide lists signs that an LLM like Claude suits a classification task better than traditional ML:

- Limited labeled data: Claude can classify with just a few dozen labeled examples
- Categories likely to change: Claude adapts without extensive relabeling
- Complex, unstructured text inputs
- Rules based on semantic understanding
- A need for interpretable reasoning
- Edge cases and ambiguous inputs
- Multilingual support without separate models

Before automating, study how people do the task today: which criteria set the SLA, which rules exist and where they fail, and how edge cases are handled. Then define a clear list of categories: Claude's routing is directly proportional to how well-defined they are. Set success criteria with measurable benchmarks and thresholds, such as 95% accuracy.

diagram.caption: The ticket-routing guide's order, from requirements to prompt.

sections.heading: Choose an approach by constraints
sections.body:
For ticket routing, the guide says model choice depends on the trade-offs between cost, accuracy and response time. Anthropic's model-selection guide describes two starting strategies:

- Efficiency-first: begin with Claude Haiku 5.5, test, and upgrade only for specific capability gaps. Best for tight latency, cost-sensitive and high-volume, straightforward tasks.
- Capability-first: begin with Claude Opus 5.5, then lower effort or downgrade models over time. Best for complex reasoning and where accuracy outweighs cost.

Either way, decide with benchmark tests specific to your use case, using your actual prompts and data.

Not every success criterion or failing eval is best solved by prompt engineering. For example, you can sometimes improve latency and cost more easily by selecting a different model.

title: The LLM app life cycle
summary: An LLM feature moves through a loop: test cases, a preliminary prompt, iterative testing and refinement, final validation, then shipping; Anthropic's content-moderation guide adds continuous evaluation in production. Models have a life cycle too, so pin model IDs, watch for deprecations, and re-test before you migrate.
keyPoints: Flow: **test cases → preliminary prompt → iterative testing and refinement → final validation → ship**.
Every Claude model ID is a **pinned snapshot**; from 4.6 on, dateless IDs are not evergreen pointers.
Pre-4.6 **aliases** such as `claude-sonnet-4-5` point to the most recent dated snapshot for that minor version.
Deprecated models still work; after the **retirement date** requests fail. Publicly released models get at least **60 days'** notice.
Migration can break requests: Claude Opus 5.5 rejects a non-default `temperature` with a **400** error.

sections.heading: Develop, evaluate, ship, keep evaluating
sections.body:
Anthropic's prompt engineering flow starts from test cases, not the prompt: write test cases, draft a preliminary prompt, iteratively test and refine it, run a final validation, then ship. Evals should mirror the real task distribution, include edge cases, and use automated grading when possible. A/B testing compares performance against a baseline model or an earlier version.

Shipping isn't the end. For content moderation in production, Anthropic recommends tracking the types of content being flagged to spot trends, and regularly assessing performance with metrics such as precision and recall, using that data to refine prompts and assessment criteria.

sections.heading: Pin model versions
sections.body:
Each Claude model ID identifies a pinned version: the underlying model stays constant for the lifetime of that ID. From the Claude 4.6 generation on, IDs are dateless, such as `claude-sonnet-5`, and each maps to a single, fixed snapshot. A common misconception is that dateless IDs route to the latest version; they don't. When an updated version is available, it ships under a new model ID.

Earlier models have dated IDs such as `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`, plus Claude API aliases such as `claude-sonnet-4-5` that point to the most recent dated snapshot for that minor version. The pinning guarantee covers model IDs, not those aliases.

Weights are fixed per ID, but serving infrastructure can change. If behavior shifts on a previously stable ID, an infrastructure update is the most likely cause.

sections.heading: Deprecation and migration
sections.body:
Lifecycle states:

- Active: fully supported and recommended
- Legacy: no more updates; may be deprecated in the future
- Deprecated: still works, with a recommended replacement and a retirement date
- Retired: no longer available; requests fail

Anthropic gives customers with active deployments at least 60 days' notice before retiring a publicly released model. Test your app with the replacement well before the retirement date, then migrate all usage. To find remaining usage, export from the Console Usage page: the CSV breaks usage down by API key and model.

Treat a migration as a code change. For example, a request to `claude-opus-5-5` must omit `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k` or leave them at their defaults, and manual thinking budgets are rejected; a rejected setting returns a 400 error.

title: Configuration management
summary: Keep configuration out of code and in the right file. Supply API keys through `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, pick the Claude Code settings scope by who a setting should affect, and remember that settings enforce while CLAUDE.md only guides.
keyPoints: The client SDKs read **`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`** automatically; store keys in a secrets manager and rotate them.
Settings precedence, highest first: **managed → command line → project local → shared project → user**.
List keys such as `permissions.allow` **merge** across settings files instead of overriding.
CLAUDE.md is **context, not enforced configuration**; settings rules are enforced by the client.
MCP scopes: **local** (default, private), **project** (`.mcp.json`, shared), **user** (all your projects, private).

sections.heading: API keys and environment variables
sections.body:
Send your API key as `Authorization: Bearer <key>` on direct HTTP requests, or set the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable and the client SDKs pick it up automatically, so `Anthropic()` needs no key argument. Store keys in a secrets manager, rotate them periodically, and disable or delete any key you suspect has leaked.

An expiration limits how long a leaked key stays usable, but it is not a substitute for secret hygiene.

sections.heading: Claude Code settings scopes
sections.body:
Claude Code reads settings from files with different scopes:

- User, `~/.claude/settings.json`: you, in every project on this machine
- Shared project, `.claude/settings.json`: everyone in the project, once you commit it
- Project local, `.claude/settings.local.json`: you, in this project only
- Managed: deployed by your organization; nothing you set overrides it, apart from a few security-sensitive exceptions

When the same key is set in several places, the highest level wins: managed, then command line (such as `--settings`), then project local, shared project and user. List keys such as `permissions.allow` combine across files instead. Environment variables aren't a level in this stack: which of a variable and its paired key applies is decided per pair.

sections.heading: CLAUDE.md versus settings
sections.body:
CLAUDE.md files are loaded into context at the start of every session. They are context, not enforced configuration: specific, concise instructions are followed more consistently, but they are not a hard enforcement layer. Files found up the directory tree are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other.

Use settings for technical enforcement, such as blocking tools, commands or file paths with `permissions.deny`, and CLAUDE.md for behavioral guidance such as code style. Settings rules are enforced by the client regardless of what Claude decides to do.

sections.heading: MCP and plugin configuration files
sections.body:
MCP servers have three scopes. Local (the default) and user servers are stored in `~/.claude.json` and stay private to you; project servers live in `.mcp.json` at the project root, which you check into version control so the team shares them. If the same server is defined in several scopes, local wins over project and project over user; fields aren't merged.

`.mcp.json` supports `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` expansion, but in a remote server's `url` and `headers` Claude Code reads credential variables such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as empty. Copy the value into a variable with a name of your own instead.

A plugin's optional manifest lives at `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`. Every other plugin file, including `skills/`, `hooks/` and `.mcp.json`, goes at the plugin root.

title: Errors, retries and rate limits
summary: Production Claude apps must read each error's type, retry only what is transient, and stay inside rate limits. The rule: back off on transient errors (500, 529 and rate-limit 429s, honoring `retry-after`); a spend-cap 429 won't clear on retry; fix the cause on other 4xx errors; log every `request-id`.
keyPoints: **401** is a problem with the API key; **403** is a valid key without permission for the resource; **404** is a missing resource.
**500** `api_error`: retry with exponential backoff. **529** `overloaded_error`: the API is temporarily overloaded across all users.
A rate-limit **429** carries `retry-after` (seconds to wait). A spend-cap 429 has none and fails until access resumes.
The API uses a **token bucket**: 60 RPM might be enforced as 1 request per second. Cache reads don't count toward ITPM on most models.
Every response has a unique **`request-id`**; include it when you contact support.

sections.heading: Reading an error
sections.body:
Errors come back as JSON with a top-level `error` object holding a `type` and `message`, plus a `request_id`. The status and type tell you what to do:

- 400 `invalid_request_error`: an issue with the format or content of your request
- 401 `authentication_error`: an issue with your API key, such as malformed, revoked or expired
- 403 `permission_error`: your key doesn't have permission for the resource
- 404 `not_found_error`: check the endpoint path and resource IDs
- 413 `request_too_large`: the request exceeds the endpoint's size limit
- 429 `rate_limit_error`: a rate limit, spend cap or Claude Code workspace limit
- 500 `api_error`: retry with exponential backoff; if it persists, contact support with the request ID
- 529 `overloaded_error`: the API is temporarily overloaded

Every response has a `request-id` header; the Python and TypeScript SDKs expose it as `_request_id`.

sections.heading: Rate limits and backing off
sections.body:
Limits are set per organization and measured in requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute (RPM, ITPM, OTPM) for each model class. Exceeding one returns a 429 that says which limit was hit, with a `retry-after` header giving the seconds to wait; earlier retries will fail.

The API uses the token bucket algorithm, so capacity replenishes continuously rather than at fixed intervals, and limits can apply over shorter periods: short bursts can trigger 429s. A sharp increase in usage can also hit acceleration limits, so ramp up gradually.

Response headers such as `anthropic-ratelimit-requests-remaining` and `-reset` show what's left. For most models only uncached input counts toward ITPM, so prompt caching raises effective throughput. A 429 with no `retry-after` and `enforced_spend_limit_reached` means the monthly spend cap; retries fail until access resumes.

sections.heading: Concurrency and streaming failures
sections.body:
For asyncio code, the Python SDK offers `AsyncAnthropic`, the same interface with calls you `await`; the `aiohttp` backend can improve async performance.

When streaming, an error can arrive after a 200 response. To recover an interrupted stream, save the content received so far and send a continuation request. On Claude 4.6 and later, put the partial response in a user message with an instruction to continue; on Claude 4.5 and earlier, it went at the start of an assistant message. Tool use and extended thinking blocks can't be partially recovered, so resume from the most recent text block.

title: Designing Claude applications
summary: Application design is choosing the simplest architecture that meets the need: a long prompt or retrieval, a live call or a batch, free text or structured output. The rule to remember: start simple, measure, and add complexity (extra calls, agents) only when it demonstrably helps.
keyPoints: Anthropic's 2024 post: a knowledge base under **200,000 tokens** (about 500 pages) can go in the prompt whole. Many current models now have **1M-token** windows.
The **Message Batches API** costs 50% less for work that doesn't need immediate replies; match results by `custom_id`, never by order.
Streaming improves perceived responsiveness; **TTFT** measures the wait before the first token.
**Citations** give verifiable passages; **JSON outputs** give schema-valid replies; the two can't be combined in one request.
Workflow patterns: **routing** for distinct input types, **parallelization** for guardrails or independent parts.

sections.heading: Long prompt, retrieval or batch?
sections.body:
Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post notes that if a knowledge base is smaller than 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages), you can include all of it in the prompt, with no need for RAG, and prompt caching makes that faster and cheaper. The post says larger knowledge bases need a more scalable solution, such as RAG, which chunks the corpus, embeds the chunks and adds the most relevant ones to the prompt at query time. Context windows have grown since: Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and other current models have a 1M-token context window.

When no one is waiting on the answer, batch processing fits: the Message Batches API processes large volumes asynchronously at 50% lower cost, and most batches finish in under 1 hour. Results can come back in any order, so always match them to requests by `custom_id`.

sections.heading: Latency and streaming
sections.body:
First engineer a prompt that works well, then reduce latency; doing it too early can hide what top performance looks like. The guide's levers:

- Choose the right model: Claude Haiku 5.5 offers the fastest response times
- Minimize prompt and output tokens; ask for sentence or paragraph counts rather than word counts
- Use `max_tokens` only as a blunt cap, since replies are cut off at the limit
- Stream responses so users see output as it arrives

Time to first token (TTFT) is the time until the first token of the response, which is particularly relevant for streaming UIs.

diagram.caption: Get the prompt working first, then apply the levers.

sections.heading: Grounded and structured output
sections.body:
Citations return the exact passages that support each claim. Set `citations.enabled=true` on every document in the request; the API guarantees valid pointers into the documents, and `cited_text` doesn't count toward output tokens.

JSON outputs (`output_config.format`) constrain replies to your schema through constrained decoding. The first request with a new schema is slower while its grammar compiles, then it's cached for 24 hours. Citations and JSON outputs are incompatible and return a 400 together.

The Files API lets you upload once and reference a `file_id`. Files can't be modified after upload: to change one, upload a new file and delete the old one. PDFs and plain text go in `document` blocks; convert types like .docx to plain text first.

sections.heading: Choosing a workflow pattern
sections.body:
Anthropic's "Building effective agents" recommends the simplest solution that works:

- Prompt chaining: fixed subtasks in sequence, trading latency for accuracy
- Routing: classify the input, then hand it to a specialized prompt or model
- Parallelization: sectioning (independent parts, such as a separate guardrail call) or voting (the same task several times)
- Orchestrator-workers: a central LLM breaks down complex tasks whose subtasks can't be predicted
- Evaluator-optimizer: one call generates, another critiques, in a loop

title: SDKs, REST, streaming and async
summary: You reach Claude over a REST API, usually through an official client SDK that handles headers, retries, types and streaming for you. Choose how to call it by asking whether a user is waiting and whether the work is real-time or bulk offline: synchronous, streaming, async/await, or the Message Batches API.
keyPoints: The Claude API is a **REST API** at `https://api.anthropic.com`; messages go to `POST /v1/messages` with auth, `anthropic-version` and `content-type` headers.
Client SDKs (Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP, Ruby) add automatic headers, types, **retries**, error handling, streaming and timeouts.
**Streaming** (`"stream": true`) sends output as server-sent events, so users see text as it's generated.
**Async/await** clients such as Python's `AsyncAnthropic` have the same interface; you `await` each call in asyncio code.
The **Message Batches API** is asynchronous bulk processing at **50%** of standard prices; most batches finish in under 1 hour.

sections.heading: The Messages REST API
sections.body:
The Claude API is a **RESTful API** at `https://api.anthropic.com`. You send JSON over HTTP: the Messages API is `POST /v1/messages`, and related endpoints include the Message Batches API (`POST /v1/messages/batches`) and the Token Counting API (`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens`).

Requests carry these headers:

- auth: `x-api-key`, or `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
- `anthropic-version`, for example `2023-06-01`
- `content-type: application/json`

The Messages API is stateless, so each request carries the full conversation you want Claude to see.

sections.heading: What the client SDKs add
sections.body:
The **client SDKs** are official, general-purpose Messages API clients for Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP and Ruby. They handle the plumbing you'd otherwise write yourself:

- automatic headers (auth, `anthropic-version`, `content-type`)
- type-safe requests and responses
- built-in retries and error handling (the Python SDK retries certain errors 2 times by default, with a short exponential backoff)
- streaming support
- request timeouts and connection management

You still send each request and handle each response. Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK and Claude Managed Agents work at a higher level, providing the agent loop and tool execution.
sections.example: Python: `client = Anthropic()` reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment by default. `client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[...])` returns a typed `Message`, and a 429 that persists after the automatic retries surfaces as `anthropic.RateLimitError`.

sections.heading: Synchronous vs streaming
sections.body:
A **synchronous** call such as `messages.create` waits and returns the whole `Message` at once.

**Streaming** (`"stream": true`) returns the response incrementally as server-sent events (SSE). The model starts sending its response before the output is complete, so your UI can render text as it arrives, which significantly improves the app's perceived responsiveness.

Streaming also matters for long requests. The Python SDK warns against a large `max_tokens` without streaming, because some networks drop idle connections, and it raises a `ValueError` when a non-streaming request is expected to take longer than about 10 minutes. If you only need the final result, stream with `.stream()` and call `.get_final_message()`.
sections.example: `with client.messages.stream(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[...]) as stream:` then `for text in stream.text_stream: print(text, end="")` shows the reply as it's generated, instead of after a long blank wait.

sections.heading: Async/await
sections.body:
**Async/await** is about how your program waits, not about Claude. The Python SDK's `AsyncAnthropic` client has the same interface as the sync `Anthropic` client, but you `await` its calls from asyncio code: `await client.messages.create(...)`, and with `stream=True` you read the events with `async for`. For better concurrency, it can use an `aiohttp` HTTP backend (`DefaultAioHttpClient`).

The reply still comes back from that same call. That's the difference from the Message Batches API, where processing is asynchronous on Anthropic's side and you poll for results later.
sections.example: `client = AsyncAnthropic()`, then inside `async def handle(q):` write `message = await client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": q}])`.

sections.heading: The Message Batches API
sections.body:
The **Message Batches API** processes large volumes of Messages requests asynchronously. You create a batch, each request in it is handled independently, and you poll for the batch's status and retrieve results once processing has ended.

- All usage is charged at **50%** of standard API prices.
- Most batches finish in under 1 hour. Results are available once every request completes or after 24 hours, and a batch expires if processing doesn't complete within 24 hours.
- A batch holds up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB; results stay available for 29 days.
- `stream: true` and fast mode aren't supported in batch requests.

It suits work that doesn't need an immediate response: large-scale evaluations, content moderation, data analysis and bulk content generation.
sections.example: Each request has a `custom_id` and the usual `params`: `client.messages.batches.create(requests=[{"custom_id": "review-1", "params": {...}}])`. When `processing_status` is `"ended"`, iterate `client.messages.batches.results(batch_id)` and check each entry's `result.type`.

sections.heading: Choosing a call style
sections.body:
Two questions decide it: is a user waiting, and is the work real-time or bulk offline?

- **A user is waiting on the reply:** stream it, so text appears as it's generated.
- **Your code only needs the finished result:** a synchronous call returns the whole `Message`; for a large `max_tokens`, stream and call `.get_final_message()`.
- **An asyncio app with many requests in flight:** use the async client and `await` each call.
- **Bulk work nobody needs right away:** the Message Batches API, at half the price, with most batches done within an hour.

These combine: an asyncio server can stream each user's reply while a nightly job sends the bulk work as a batch.
sections.example: A chat UI streams each reply. A FastAPI backend awaits its calls with `AsyncAnthropic`. A nightly job scoring 50,000 product reviews goes through the Message Batches API at 50% of the standard price.

title: Streaming without corrupting state
summary: With `"stream": true`, a response arrives as a sequence of server-sent events instead of one finished `Message`, so your handler builds the message up piece by piece. Collect each block's deltas and act only after that block's `content_block_stop`. A stream ending is not the same as a message completing: check `stop_reason` from `message_delta` before you trust the result.
keyPoints: Order: `message_start` → per block `content_block_start`, deltas, `content_block_stop` → `message_delta` → `message_stop`, with `ping` events anywhere.
`input_json_delta` fragments are **partial JSON strings**: accumulate them and parse once that block's `content_block_stop` arrives.
`stop_reason` is `null` in `message_start` and arrives in `message_delta`, whose `usage` counts are **cumulative**.
An error event can arrive mid-stream; `tool_use` and `thinking` blocks can't be partially recovered.
Never save a partial assistant turn as if it were finished: completion needs `message_stop` **and** a `stop_reason` you've handled.

sections.heading: What streaming changes
sections.body:
**Streaming** means setting `"stream": true` on a Messages request so the response arrives incrementally as **server-sent events** (SSE). Users see text as it's generated instead of waiting for the whole reply.

The trade-off is that you no longer receive one complete `Message` object. You receive many small events, and your code has to assemble them into content blocks, each identified by an `index` that matches its position in the final `content` array. Until the last event arrives, everything you hold is provisional.

If you don't need the text as it arrives, the SDKs can stream internally and hand you the finished `Message` through an accumulation helper such as `stream.get_final_message()` (TypeScript: `stream.finalMessage()`).
sections.example: A chat UI prints each `text_delta` as it arrives, so the user sees "Hello" and then "!" appear. Meanwhile, the handler adds both pieces to block 0, so that once the stream completes it holds the full text "Hello!" to store in the conversation history.

sections.heading: The event sequence and what to do with each
sections.body:
Every stream follows the same flow. Here's what a handler does at each step:

- `message_start`: create an empty message. It holds a `Message` with empty `content`, and `stop_reason` is `null`.
- `content_block_start`: open a new block at the given `index` (`text`, `tool_use` or `thinking`).
- `content_block_delta`: append the fragment to the block at that `index` (`text_delta`, `input_json_delta`, `thinking_delta` or `signature_delta`).
- `content_block_stop`: mark that block complete. Only now is it safe to use.
- `message_delta`: record the top-level changes, including `stop_reason`. Its `usage` token counts are cumulative, so replace your total rather than adding to it.
- `message_stop`: the final event. The message is done.

`ping` events can appear anywhere, and new event types may be added, so handle unknown types gracefully.

diagram.caption: One stream: a message wrapper around one or more content blocks.

sections.heading: Don't act on a partial block
sections.body:
A delta is a fragment, not a value. For `tool_use` blocks, the deltas are **partial JSON strings** (`input_json_delta`), whereas the final `tool_use.input` is always an object. Accumulate the strings and parse the JSON once you receive that block's `content_block_stop`. Parsing or executing earlier means running a tool on half an argument.

The same applies to thinking: a `thinking` block's `signature` arrives as a single `signature_delta` just before its `content_block_stop`, so a thinking block saved before then is missing its signature.

Route every delta by its `index`. A text block and a tool block in the same response stream as separate indexes and must be assembled separately. The SDK streaming helpers do this for you, and in the Python and TypeScript SDKs they can also give you the parsed `input` incrementally.
sections.example: Block 1 opens as `tool_use` named `get_weather` with `"input": {}`. Deltas then arrive: `{"location":`, ` "San`, ` Francisc`, `o,`, ` CA"}`. Only after `content_block_stop` for index 1 does the joined string parse to `{"location": "San Francisco, CA"}`. That's the moment to run the tool.

sections.heading: When the stream stops early
sections.body:
Streams can stop before they finish. The API may send an **error event** mid-stream (for example `overloaded_error`, which would be an HTTP 529 without streaming), and networks drop connections. So **track completion on purpose**: record which blocks reached `content_block_stop`, whether a `message_delta` delivered a `stop_reason`, and whether `message_stop` arrived.

On an interrupted stream, **don't save the partial assistant turn** to history as if it were a finished reply. `tool_use` and `thinking` blocks can't be partially recovered, so never execute or store a half-built one.

If you want to resume rather than retry, the docs give a pattern: save what you received, then send a continuation request. For Claude 4.6 and later models, put the partial text in a **user** message that asks Claude to continue. For Claude 4.5 and earlier, use it to start a new assistant message. You can resume from the most recent text block.
sections.example: The connection drops after block 0 (text) completed and while block 1 (`tool_use`) was still streaming. Your handler doesn't call the tool and doesn't append an assistant message to history. It retries the request, or, on Claude Opus 5.5, it resumes by sending the received text in a user message that says the previous response was interrupted and asks Claude to continue.

sections.heading: A stream ending is not a message completing
sections.body:
Getting `message_stop` means the stream closed cleanly, not that the answer is usable. Check `stop_reason` from `message_delta` before you act:

- `end_turn`: Claude finished naturally, so use the response.
- `tool_use`: run the tool and return the result.
- `max_tokens`: the reply hit your limit and is truncated. If the last block is an incomplete `tool_use`, retry with a higher `max_tokens`.
- `refusal`: Claude declined, and this still arrives as a normal HTTP 200.
- `pause_turn`: a server-tool loop hit its iteration limit, so send the content back to continue.

A connection that just goes quiet, with no `message_stop` at all, isn't a completed message either.
sections.example: A stream closes with `message_delta` carrying `"stop_reason": "max_tokens"` and then `message_stop`. The final block is a `tool_use` whose JSON was cut off. Your handler treats the response as incomplete: no tool call, no history update. It retries with a larger `max_tokens`.

title: Defining done: evals and a calibrated judge
summary: Before a Claude feature ships, write down what done, safe and affordable mean, then turn it into an eval: input cases, expected behaviors and grading logic. Grade each check with the fastest reliable method (code where possible, a calibrated LLM judge where necessary), favor coverage over hand-graded perfection, and improve in a loop: run, read failures, change, rerun.
keyPoints: An **eval** is a set of input cases with grading logic that defines what a feature must do. Write it **before** shipping, edge cases included.
The course's **design document** states success criteria, failure handling, a **cost and latency budget** and the **trust boundary**.
Match the grader to the output: **exact or string match** for fixed answers, **code checks** for rules, an **LLM judge** for nuance.
Calibrate a judge: a clear rubric per dimension, verdicts compared with **expert human grades**, transcripts read, then occasional human review.
**Volume over quality**: more cases with slightly noisier automated grading beat a few hand-graded ones. Claude can help write the extra cases.

sections.heading: The design document: done, safe, affordable
sections.body:
Before building, the course has you write a short design document that answers four questions:

- **Success criteria:** what done means, stated so it can be measured. Anthropic's guide asks for criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant.
- **Failure handling:** what the feature does with bad input, such as empty, irrelevant or overly long messages.
- **Cost and latency budget:** Anthropic lists latency (the acceptable response time) and price (your budget for running the model) as success criteria in their own right, so they get targets too.
- **Trust boundary:** which inputs are untrusted, and what the feature is able to reach. Anthropic supervises what an agent is *able* to do by enforcing access boundaries, not only what it's told: an agent with read-only database access can be deployed far more broadly than one that writes to prod.

Each line should become something an eval can check.
sections.example: A returns bot. Success: the correct policy answer on a labeled test set. Failure handling: empty or off-topic messages get a short apology and a help link. Budget: a target response time and a monthly spend limit. Trust boundary: customer messages are untrusted, and the bot gets read-only access to orders, so no instruction is needed to stop it editing them.

sections.heading: An eval defines done before you ship
sections.body:
An eval is a test for an AI system: give it an input, then apply grading logic to the output. A set of these cases, each with the behavior you expect, defines what the feature must do before it ships. Without one, debugging is reactive: wait for complaints, reproduce, fix, and hope nothing else regressed.

Anthropic's design principles:

- **Be task-specific:** mirror your real-world task distribution, and don't forget edge cases such as irrelevant or nonexistent input, overly long input, and ambiguous cases where even humans would struggle to agree.
- **Automate when possible:** structure cases for automated grading (multiple-choice, string match, code-graded, LLM-graded).
- **Get help writing cases:** writing hundreds of test cases by hand is hard, so have Claude generate more from a baseline set. The course adds: ask the model to list the edge cases that could break the current implementation.
sections.example: You have 25 hand-written cases for a contract summarizer. Give them to Claude and ask for a few hundred more in the same style, plus the inputs most likely to break the prompt: an empty contract, a very long one, a contract that has nothing to do with the task, and a clause two lawyers would read differently.

sections.heading: Match the grader to the output's shape
sections.body:
Choose the fastest, most reliable, most scalable method that can judge the output. Anthropic recommends deterministic graders where possible and LLM graders where necessary.

- **Exact match** (`output == golden_answer`): the whole output must equal the answer, typically after normalizing whitespace and case. Ideal for clear-cut, categorical answers such as a sentiment label.
- **String match** (`key_phrase in output`): one known string must appear, whatever else is said.
- **Code-graded checks:** rules written in code, such as "parses as JSON and `priority` holds an allowed value". Fast, cheap, objective and reproducible, but brittle to valid variations and short on nuance.
- **LLM-as-judge:** a model grades against a rubric. Fast, flexible and scalable for complex judgment such as tone, but non-deterministic and in need of calibration.

Human grading is the most flexible and high quality, but slow and expensive: avoid it where you can, and use it to calibrate the judge.
sections.example: One support-bot eval, three graders: the routed team name is checked by exact match, the reply must contain the ticket ID (string match), and the tone of the reply is scored 1–5 by an LLM judge against a target tone.

sections.heading: Build and calibrate the judge
sections.body:
A judge's scores are only defensible if they agree with the people whose judgment the judge stands in for.

- **Clear rubric:** vague rubrics produce inconsistent judgments. With several qualities, write a rubric for each dimension and grade each with an isolated judge, not one judge for everything.
- **Specific output:** ask for only "correct" or "incorrect", or a 1–5 score. Purely qualitative comments are hard to assess quickly and at scale.
- **Reasoning first:** a grader with thinking on reasons before it scores, which improves grading on complex judgments.
- **A way out:** let the judge return "Unknown" when it lacks the information, to reduce hallucinated verdicts.
- **Calibrate against people:** have experts grade a sample, compare their verdicts with the judge's, and refine until they rarely diverge. Test reliability before you scale; once it's robust, occasional human review is usually enough.
- **Read transcripts:** they show whether a failure is a real mistake or the grader rejecting a valid answer.

It's generally best practice to grade with a different model from the one that produced the output.
sections.example: Experts and the judge grade the same 100 replies and disagree mostly on partly correct ones. The rubric only said "resolves the issue", so you add how a partial answer is graded, recheck the same sample, and scale up only once the verdicts closely agree.

sections.heading: Coverage over perfection, and the loop
sections.body:
More cases with slightly lower-signal automated grading beat fewer high-quality, hand-graded ones: coverage usually reveals more than a few perfect grades.

The course puts the pieces together as a loop: set a goal, write an initial prompt, run the eval, read where it failed, apply one prompt-engineering change, and run the eval again. Rerun the whole set, not just the failures, so a fix that breaks other cases shows up.

When scores look wrong, suspect the eval too:

- A **0% pass rate** across many trials usually signals a broken task, not an incapable agent. A reference solution, a known output that passes all graders, proves the task is solvable and the graders are configured correctly.
- **Overly strict verifiers** reject correct responses over spurious differences like formatting. Fix the grader, not the model.
sections.example: First run: 14 of 200 cases fail, and the transcripts show most are long contracts where the summary skips the termination clause. You add one instruction about termination terms and rerun all 200: those cases now pass, and nothing that passed before fails.
